===San Diego Chargers===
Tolliver was selected by the [[San Diego Chargers]] in the second round of the [[1989 NFL draft]] with the 51st overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1989 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1989/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-26 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The Chargers traded third, fourth, and seventh-round picks in exchange for the [[New York Giants]]' second-round pick in order to draft him.<ref>{{cite news|first=Frank|last=Litsky|title=Giants' Rookie Rejoins Practice|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/10/19/sports/giants-rookie-rejoins-practice.html|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 19, 1989|access-date=December 29, 2007}}</ref> Tolliver was signed on July 31, 1989, after a short holdout.<ref>{{cite news|title=Tolliver, Chargers reach 4–year, $1.3 million deal|work=[[Austin American-Statesman]]|page=D3|date=July 31, 1989}}</ref> He was to compete with [[Mark Malone]] and [[David Archer (quarterback)|David Archer]] for the starting job, a spot which eventually went to [[Jim McMahon]] after the Chargers traded for him. As the 1989 season began with McMahon at the helm, Tolliver was slated to play the second half of the final preseason game against the [[Phoenix Cardinals]]. After 13 completions in 23 attempts, Tolliver ran the ball late in the game and broke his [[collarbone]], sidelining him for at least six weeks.<ref>{{cite news|first=Don|last=Patterson|title=Tolliver, McKnight Out for at Least Six Weeks|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|page=3|date=March 3, 1989}}</ref> After spending the first seven games on the [[injured reserve list]], Tolliver was taken off the list and named the starter for the game against the [[Seattle Seahawks]] on October 29, replacing McMahon who had disappointed at quarterback.<ref>{{cite news|first=Bob|last=Wolf|title=Chargers Readying Tolliver for Start Against Seahawks|work=Los Angeles Times|date=October 26, 1989|page=1}}</ref> In Tolliver's first start, he played three quarters, throwing six completed passes in 17 attempts for 41 yards and throwing an interception in a 10–7 loss.<ref>{{cite news|first=Brian|last=Hewitt|title=Chargers Again Lack a Finishing Touch|work=Los Angeles Times|date=October 30, 1989|page=1}}</ref> Tolliver subsequently lost the starting job back to McMahon. However, in late November, Tolliver was given the starting job back, remaining the starting quarterback the rest of the season. Tolliver finished the season having played five games with 89 completions in 185 attempts, 1097 yards, five touchdowns, eight interceptions, and a 57.9 quarterback rating.<ref name=pfr>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TollBi00.htm|title=Billy Joe Tolliver Statistics|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference, LLC|access-date=December 29, 2007}}</ref>

As the 1990 season began, McMahon was released by the team, leaving Tolliver as the starting quarterback at [[training camp]]. After training camp and a preseason in which Tolliver started and was relieved by quarterbacks [[Mark Vlasic]] and rookie [[John Friesz]], Chargers head coach [[Dan Henning]] named Vlasic as the starting quarterback against the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in the season opener, saying that he was "steadier" than Tolliver.<ref>{{cite news|title=Morris, Carter Axed; Dallas Gets Highsmith; Several Holdouts Sign Around NFL|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=September 4, 1989}}</ref> After a loss against Dallas, Tolliver regained his starting job during the game two against the [[Cincinnati Bengals]]. Despite some shaky performances in the following weeks, the Chargers' coaching staff stuck by their quarterback, saying that "the last thing we need around here is more change."<ref>{{cite news|title=A Few Fun Facts Sure to Amaze and Mystify|work=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|page=D5|date=November 2, 1990}}</ref> Tolliver played nearly the rest of the season as the starting quarterback but was replaced by Friesz for the final game of the season against the [[Los Angeles Raiders]]. The Chargers made this move because, according to Henning, "Tolliver has to work on his shortcomings."<ref>{{cite news|first=T.J.|last=Simers|title=Friesz to Replace Tolliver as Chargers' Starter|work=Los Angeles Times|page=1|date=December 25, 1990}}</ref> Tolliver finished the season having completed 216 of 410 passes, thrown for 2,574 yards, 16 touchdowns, and 16 interceptions, and posting a QB rating of 68.9.<ref name=pfr/>

Although Tolliver had the confidence of Dan Henning, Chargers general manager [[Bobby Beathard]] and owner [[Alex Spanos]] were unsatisfied with his production during the 1990 season, and were looking towards Friesz as the future quarterback.<ref>{{cite news|first=Jay|last=Lawrence|title=Hot Quarterback Gives Raiders Hope in Playoffs|work=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]]|page=8D|date=January 9, 1991}}</ref> Tolliver was the leading man for the starting quarterback position as training camp for the 1991 season began, with Friesz battling [[Bob Gagliano]] for the backup spot. However, after training camp ended, Friesz was named the starting quarterback for the 1991 season opener against the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Chargers Switch QBs|work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|page=D11|date=August 25, 1991}}</ref>

===Atlanta Falcons===
Just a few days after losing the starting job, Tolliver was traded to the [[Atlanta Falcons]] for a fifth-round draft pick.<ref>{{cite news|title=Transactions|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/08/29/sports/transactions-260691.html|work=The New York Times|date=August 29, 1991|access-date=December 30, 2007}}</ref> In Atlanta, Tolliver was the backup quarterback behind [[Chris Miller (quarterback)|Chris Miller]] and alongside rookie [[Brett Favre]], and played part of seven games throughout the season. Tolliver's breakthrough as a Falcon came against the [[San Francisco 49ers]] on November 3. Miller was injured in the second quarter, and Tolliver was brought in for the rest of the game. With one second left, he threw a 44-yard [[Hail Mary pass]] to [[Michael Haynes (wide receiver)|Michael Haynes]], which was caught for a touchdown and sealing a 17–14 upset victory.<ref>{{cite news|title=Tolliver's Falcon debut shows a little rust and a lot of luck|work=[[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]]|page=B6|date=November 4, 1991}}</ref> Due to his performance and Miller's injury, Tolliver was given his first start the following week against the [[Washington Redskins]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Falcons' battered offense will need more miracles vs. Redskins|work=Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=F1|date=November 10, 1991}}</ref> Tolliver's first start with the Falcons was a 56–17 blowout loss. Afterwards, Tolliver got his second and last start of the season against the [[Green Bay Packers]] as a result of Miller suddenly running a fever.<ref>{{cite news|title=Miller leads feverish rally; Sick QB enters in second half, hurls 2 TD passes|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=E7|date=December 2, 1991}}</ref> Tolliver finished the regular season having completing 40 of 82 passes with four touchdowns, two interceptions, and a QB rating of 75.8.<ref name=pfr/>

After the Falcons traded Favre to the Packers, Miller and Tolliver were the only quarterbacks on the roster. Before the season started, [[Wade Wilson (American football)|Wade Wilson]] signed with the team, and the two shared the role of backup to Miller. Tolliver played two of the first eight games, then was named the starting quarterback when the Falcons lost Miller for the season as a result of [[reconstructive surgery]] on his left knee.<ref>{{cite news|title=Falcons' Miller Out For Season|work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]|page=E3|date=November 3, 1992}}</ref> Tolliver's first start of the season came against the 49ers. He completed 16 of 25 passes, but threw three interceptions in a 41–3 loss.<ref>{{cite news|first=Nancy|last=Gay|title=Blowout II 49ers Rip Falcons for Second Time in Three Weeks, Set Up Showdown with Saints|work=[[San Jose Mercury News]]|page=1D|date=November 10, 1992}}</ref> The next week against the Cardinals, Tolliver was benched for the final series as Wilson led the team to victory and Tolliver argued with coach [[Jerry Glanville]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Falcons Drive Past the Cardinals, 20–17 NFC: Wilson comes off bench to lead Atlanta on game-winning march against Phoenix|work=Los Angeles Times|page=C5|date=November 16, 1992}}</ref> Despite the conflict and a shoulder injury, Glanville gave Tolliver the start the following week against the [[Buffalo Bills]]. He played a few more games before being replaced by Wilson for the rest of the season, partially as a result of Wilson throwing five touchdown passes in his first start en route to a 35–7 Falcons victory.<ref>{{cite news|title=Surprise starter Wilson modestly takes 5 TD passes in stride|work=Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=D6|date=December 14, 1992}}</ref> Tolliver finished the season with five touchdowns, five interceptions, a 55.7% completion percentage, and a 70.4 QB rating.<ref name=pfr/>

After the 1992 season, Tolliver was a restricted [[free agent]]. Wilson signed a contract with the Saints, and to replace him the Falcons signed [[Bobby Hebert]]. Tolliver signed a one-year contract in August, after holding out for a time.<ref>{{cite news|title=Tolliver agrees to 1–year deal; Conner is last holdout left|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=C8|date=August 7, 1993}}</ref> Tolliver started the 1993 season as the third-string quarterback behind Hebert and Miller. However, Miller re-injured his left knee in late September, making Tolliver the main backup to Hebert.<ref>{{cite news|title=Falcons Notebook; With Miller out, Tolliver rises to No. 2 quarterback|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=E3|date=September 30, 1993}}</ref> Tolliver made his first start against the [[Los Angeles Rams]], but was injured in his second start against the Saints; the Falcons signed [[Chris Hakel]] as a result of the injury.<ref>{{cite news|title=Falcons Release Stephens and Add Two Players|work=The Philadelphia Inquirer|page=D02|date=October 27, 1993}}</ref> Tolliver finished the season in occasional relief for Hebert, who remained bothered by injuries. Over the course of the year, Tolliver played in seven games and threw for just under 500 yards, and became a free agent after the season ended.<ref name=pfr/>

===Houston Oilers===
In early September 1994, Tolliver was signed to a contract by the [[Houston Oilers]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Campbell|first=Steve|title=Oilers find use for SWC; For Houston, league is a quarterback haven|date=September 8, 1994|work=[[Fort Worth Star-Telegram]]|page=1}}</ref> He was originally the third-string quarterback, but ineffectiveness by [[Bucky Richardson]] led Tolliver to relieve him in a game against the [[Cleveland Browns]]. Tolliver played well enough to be considered for the starting job the following week due to [[Cody Carlson]] dealing with injuries.<ref>{{cite news|first=Mike|last=Lutz|title=Oilers' Tolliver might start against Eagles|work=Fort Worth Star-Telegram|page=5|date=October 21, 1994}}</ref> Tolliver made his first start in a game against the Raiders, but played inconsistently over seven starts and was replaced by Richardson in the season finale against the [[New York Jets]]. After finishing the season, Tolliver became a free agent and left the NFL.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/12/22/sports/pro-football-hasty-is-wearing-the-frustration-of-the-jets-failure-on-his-sleeve.html|title=Pro Football; Hasty Is Wearing the Frustration of the Jets' Failure on His Sleeve|work=[[The New York Times]]|first=Gerald|last=Eskanazi|date=December 22, 1994|access-date=December 21, 2013}}</ref>

===Shreveport Pirates===
Tolliver signed a three-year contract worth about $1 million with the [[Shreveport Pirates]] of the [[Canadian Football League]]  before the 1995 season began.<ref>{{cite news|first=Steve|last=Yount|title=Morning News Roundup|work=[[Dallas Morning News]]|date=March 16, 1995}}</ref> Early in the season, Tolliver got to compete against former teammate David Archer in the [[San Antonio Texans]]' CFL debut.<ref>{{cite news|title=QBs Tolliver, Archer face each other today|work=Austin American-Statesman|date=July 1, 1995|page=E7}}</ref> He finished the season having thrown for 3,767 yards, 16 touchdowns, and 15 interceptions.<ref name=cfl>{{cite news|title=Falcons Are Likely to Go with Tolliver|work=The Sacramento Bee|date=September 20, 1997|page=C8}}</ref> After the team folded following a 5–13 season, Tolliver was again without a team.

===Atlanta Falcons (second stint)===
In October 1996, Tolliver rejoined the Falcons as the third-string quarterback, this time sitting behind [[Bobby Hebert]] and [[Browning Nagle]].<ref>{{cite news|title=No varsity? Falcons call in 'B' team; Billy Joe joins Bobby, Browning on QB list|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=G3|date=October 24, 1996}}</ref> He spent the 1996 season on the bench, and did not take a snap in a game. He was re-signed by Atlanta in April and given a one-year contract worth $325,000.<ref>{{cite news|title=Tolliver back for Falcons|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=E10|date=March 20, 1997}}</ref>

Tolliver was slated to compete with [[Tommy Maddox]] for the backup quarterback spot at Atlanta as training camp rolled around. Halfway through August, Maddox was released, and Tolliver was made the primary backup behind [[Chris Chandler (American football)|Chris Chandler]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Falcons release Maddox, 16 others; Long relationship ends with Reeves|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|page=E1|date=August 19, 1997}}</ref> Tolliver played his first NFL game since 1994 on September 7, 1997, against the [[Carolina Panthers]]. He completed 7 of 17 passes for 79 yards.<ref>{{cite news|first=David|last=Newton|title=Panthers Notes|work=[[The State (newspaper)|The State]]|page=C8|date=September 8, 1997}}</ref> After relieving Chandler again the following week, Tolliver was slated to start the next game against the 49ers, in what became his only starting appearance of the season.<ref name=cfl/> He was slated to start again against the [[Denver Broncos]], but instead came in late in the game. He was almost able to lead the Falcons to a comeback victory over the Broncos, completing six of nine passes for 85 yards and a touchdown, but he instead lost to the then-undefeated Broncos as the team remained winless.<ref>{{cite news|first=Alex|last=Marvez|title=Elway's Revenge Incomplete Reeves' Falcons Stay Surprisingly Close But Denver Still Unbeaten|work=[[Rocky Mountain News]]|date=September 29, 1997|page=2}}</ref> When Chandler went down with an injury in late October, coach [[Dan Reeves]] chose to start [[Tony Graziani]]. Shortly afterwards, Tolliver was released by the Falcons.<ref>{{cite news|title=Tolliver Waived, Miller Signed|work=[[The Miami Herald]]|page=8D|date=October 28, 1997}}</ref>

===Kansas City Chiefs===
In early November, Kansas City Chiefs quarterback [[Elvis Grbac]] was lost for the season due to a broken collarbone. As a result, the Chiefs signed Tolliver to a two-year contract as the third-string quarterback to replace him.<ref>{{cite news|title=Chiefs Sign QB Tolliver|work=[[The Wichita Eagle]]|page=3C|date=November 6, 1997}}</ref> Tolliver finished the season having completed 64 passes in 116 attempts for 677 yards, five touchdowns, and one interception. Only one of the 116 attempts came as a Kansas City quarterback.<ref name=pfr/> The 1998 preseason began with Tolliver competing with Pat Barnes for the third-string quarterback job, but this ended when Tolliver was released by the Chiefs in August.<ref>{{cite news|first=Adam|last=Teicher|title=Tolliver loses out in QB competition|work=[[Kansas City Star]]|page=C7|date=August 25, 1998}}</ref>

===New Orleans Saints===
After Saints quarterback [[Billy Joe Hobert]] was lost for the season with a ruptured [[Achilles tendon]], the Saints signed Tolliver to a two-year deal.<ref>{{cite news|title=Sports Briefly|work=Fort Worth Star-Telegram|page=12|date=September 10, 1998}}</ref> After four starts by [[Danny Wuerffel]], Saints coach [[Mike Ditka]] gave Tolliver the start against the Atlanta Falcons.<ref>{{cite news|first=Tom|last=Silverstein|title=Broncos are hitting on all cylinders; Play of backups, Davis have fans talking 16–0|work=[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]]|date=October 16, 1998|page=7C|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1683&dat=19981016&id=WKcaAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Li8EAAAAIBAJ&pg=4204,705706|access-date=November 15, 2015|archive-date=November 17, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117040610/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1683&dat=19981016&id=WKcaAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Li8EAAAAIBAJ&pg=4204,705706|url-status=dead}}</ref> After starting for four weeks and having a few impressive performances, Tolliver was benched in favor of [[Kerry Collins]], who finished the season as starting quarterback.<ref>{{cite news|first=Mary|last=Foster|title=Collins Moves into Standing QB Slot|work=[[The Charlotte Observer]]|page=4B|date=November 12, 1998}}</ref> Tolliver finished the year with one of his most statistically impressive seasons, completing 110 of 199 passes for 1,427 yards, eight touchdowns, four interceptions, and finishing with a QB rating of 83.1.<ref name=pfr/>

Tolliver started the 1999 season as Hobert's backup. Hobert started the first four games but was injured, leaving Tolliver to start against the [[Tennessee Titans]] on October 17 and the Giants the week after. Hobert started the next game, but suffered a [[pinched nerve]] in his neck, resulting in Tolliver's third start of the season against the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Steve|last=Wiseman|title=Saints Can't Buck Injury Bug Hobert Will Miss Tampa Bay|work=[[The Sun Herald]]|page=C6|date=November 4, 1999}}</ref> Against the 49ers, he scored the third and fourth rushing touchdowns of his career en route to a 24–6 win.<ref>{{cite news|first=T.J.|last=Simers|title=Rewind Week 10; Lightning Bolt May Strike Any Time|work=Los Angeles Times|page=3|date=November 16, 1999}}</ref> However, the next week against the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], Tolliver suffered a torn [[medial collateral ligament|MCL]], and he was considered likely to miss the rest of the season.<ref>{{cite news|first=Steve|last=Wiseman|title=Injures QB May Be Out Rest of Season Severity of Injury Not Known Yet|work=The Sun Herald|page=D6|date=November 22, 1999}}</ref> A couple of weeks later, Tolliver had bounced back from his injury by "treating himself with some [[WD-40]]" and was named the starter in the December 12 game against the [[St. Louis Rams]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Jeff|last=Gordon|title=Tolliver and Saints are Set to Battle the Rams|work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch|page=5|date=December 11, 1999}}</ref> Tolliver was again injured the following week against the [[Baltimore Ravens]], putting an end to his season, which he finished with a  51.9 completion percentage, 1,916 yards, seven touchdowns, 16 interceptions, and a QB rating of 58.9.<ref name=pfr/>

Throughout the 1999 season, Tolliver remained a vocal supporter of coach Ditka despite the Saints' 3–13 record, saying "I think he's a heck of a football coach, a great motivator. We just got to start buying what he's selling."<ref>{{cite news|title=The NFC|work=Kansas City Star|page=2|date=December 19, 1999}}</ref> Ditka was fired by the Saints, but as training camp for the 2000 season began, Tolliver was the Saints' backup quarterback behind [[Jeff Blake]]. On August 1, the Saints traded for quarterback [[Aaron Brooks (American football)|Aaron Brooks]], which left Tolliver to compete for the third-string spot alongside [[Jake Delhomme]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Steve|last=Wiseman|title=Saints Work Fast to Make Fix|work=The Sun Herald|page=D1|date=August 1, 2000}}</ref> The Saints' roster was reduced to 53 players, and Tolliver was among those cut.<ref>{{cite news|first=Steve|last=Wiseman|title=Saints, Tolliver Part Ways Veteran QB Among Cuts|work=The Sun Herald|page=D1|date=August 28, 2000}}</ref> When the Saints lost Jeff Blake for the season in mid-November due to a dislocated foot, Tolliver was re-signed by the Saints, though he did not play a game that season.<ref>{{cite news|title=Saints' Blake Out for Rest of Season|work=[[The Bradenton Herald]]|page=4|date=November 21, 2000}}</ref>

===Green Bay Packers===
In July 2001, Tolliver was signed by the Green Bay Packers. This briefly reunited him with Brett Favre, with whom he was teammates in Atlanta. However, he was cut on August 21, 2001, when [[Doug Pederson]] won the backup job, and this stint marked the end of Tolliver's professional career.<ref name=packers>{{cite web|url=http://www.packers.com/news/releases/2001/07/07-17.html|title=Packers Sign Veteran Quarterback Billy Joe Tolliver as Free Agent|publisher=Green Bay Packers Press Release|work=Packers.com|date=July 17, 2001|access-date=May 16, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090426235747/http://www.packers.com/news/releases/2001/07/07-17.html|archive-date=April 26, 2009}}</ref><ref name="2001 bio">{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021019000115/http://www.packers.com/team/players/tolliver_billy_joe/|archive-date=October 19, 2002|title=Billy Joe Tolliver #11|publisher=Green Bay Packers|url=http://www.packers.com/team/players/tolliver_billy_joe/|access-date=February 11, 2019|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Tolliver was named after his uncle Joe and aunt Billie.<ref>{{cite news|first=Kevin|last=Sherrington|title=Fast-Lane QB To Lead Texas Tech's High-Gear Attack|work=The Dallas Morning News|date=August 18, 1986}}</ref> He and his wife, Sheila, have five children.<ref name=packers/>

Tolliver is an avid [[golf]]er and has played many celebrity tournaments. He is a regular competitor at the [[American Century Championship]] in Lake Tahoe,<ref>{{cite news|date=July 13, 2007|title=Ex-NFL QB Tolliver leads Tahoe celebrity golf|work=[[USA Today]]|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/golf/2007-07-13-tahoe-golf_N.htm|access-date=January 1, 2008}}</ref> the annual competition to determine the best golfers among American sports and entertainment celebrities. He won in 1996, when it was the Isuzu Celebrity Golf Challenge,<ref name=packers/> in 2005, in 2010 (with a new point record of 84 points), and in 2013, and had a total of fourteen top-ten finishes as of the 2019 tournament.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://americancenturychampionship.com/top-ten-performances-american-century-championship/ |title=Top Ten Performances – 1990–2019 |publisher=American Century Championship|access-date=December 22, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Justin|last=Scacco|url=https://www.recordcourier.com/news/tony-romo-repeats-at-american-century-championship/|title=Tony Romo repeats at American Century Championship|work=Record-Courier|date=July 15, 2019|access-date=December 22, 2019|archive-date=December 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191222191907/https://www.recordcourier.com/news/tony-romo-repeats-at-american-century-championship/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''Billy Joe Hobert''' (born January 8, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily as a [[substitution (sport)|reserve]].<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20111121122617/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=HOBERBIL01 Billy Hobert]}}. databasefootball.com</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Washington Huskies football|Washington Huskies]].

==College career==
While at the [[University of Washington]], Hobert led the [[Washington Huskies football|Huskies]] to a [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championship]] in [[1991 Washington Huskies football team|1991]], during his [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]] sophomore season.  He was elevated to the [[Starting lineup|starting]] position after junior [[Mark Brunell]] suffered a serious knee injury during spring drills, causing him to miss most of the 1991 season. During the 1991 season, Hobert was 173/285 on completions for 2,271 yards with 22 touchdowns versus 10 interceptions, with 56 yards rushing and 5 touchdowns.<ref>{{cite web |title=1991 Washington Football Stats |url=http://www.totalfootballstats.com/Team_College.asp?id=166&Season=1991 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111101073718/http://www.totalfootballstats.com/Team_College.asp?id=166&Season=1991 |archive-date=November 1, 2011 |access-date=November 17, 2011 |website=Total Football Stats}}</ref>

After the success of the 1991 season, Hobert became implicated in a major [[NCAA]] scandal. It was revealed he had received a series of loans totaling $50,000 made by the father-in-law of a friend,<ref name=srstbln>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ENVYAAAAIBAJ&sjid=QfADAAAAIBAJ&pg=6372%2C5503134 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |last1=Farrey |first1=Tom |last2=Nalder |first2=Eric |agency=(Seattle Times)|title=Hobert blows $50,000 loan |date=November 6, 1992 |page=C1}}</ref><ref name=nytarch>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/11/06/sports/college-football-huskies-suspend-hobert-after-learning-of-loans.html |work=New York Times |title=College Football: Huskies suspend Hobert after learning of loans |date=November 6, 1992 |access-date=October 6, 2017}}</ref> while Hobert himself had no assets and no specific payment {{nowrap|schedule.<ref name=ST062002>{{cite news |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20020620/hobert20/billy-joe-hobert-villain-hero-debate-rages |first=Les |last=Carpenter  |title=Billy Joe Hobert: Villain, hero? Debate rages |work=Seattle Times |date=June 20, 2002 |access-date=October 6, 2017}}</ref><ref name=borsdo>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ENVYAAAAIBAJ&sjid=QfADAAAAIBAJ&pg=6971%2C5528044 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |last1=Borst |first=Don |agency=(McClatchy News Service)|title=Hobert takes plunge from lofty perch |date=November 6, 1992 |page=C7}}</ref>}} The story broke in early November [[1992 Washington Huskies football team|1992]], when the top-ranked Huskies were {{nowrap|8–0}} and on a 22-game winning {{nowrap|streak;<ref name=srstbln/><ref name=winoisb>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_EFWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=fuoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=1313%2C262599|work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=Washington is No. 1 in Stanford's book |date=November 1, 1992 |page=1E}}</ref><ref name=boostan>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=DNVYAAAAIBAJ&sjid=QfADAAAAIBAJ&pg=1754%2C3214801 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |agency=Associated Press |title=Blowout of Stanford moves Huskies to No. 1 in AP poll |date=November 2, 1992 |page=C1}}</ref>}} they lost three of four games to finish {{nowrap|9–3.<ref name=wc1mnrp>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=P0RWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=beoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=4056%2C401432 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |last=Bonk |first=Thomas |agency=(Los Angeles Times)|title=Wheatley conducts 1-man Rose parade past Huskies |date=January 2, 1993 |page=1D }}</ref>}}

This cost Hobert his college eligibility, and was an aggravating factor in the university receiving [[Pacific-10 Conference]] sanctions for lack of institutional control; it led to head coach [[Don James (American football)|Don James]] resigning in protest in August [[1993 Washington Huskies football team|1993]] over a two-year bowl ban.<ref name=ST062002/><ref name=itjdfw>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=mZ8nAAAAIBAJ&sjid=eOoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6850%2C5126464 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon|agency=Associated Press |title=It's judgment day for Washington |date=August 22, 1993 |page=8E}}</ref><ref name=phjres>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=mp8nAAAAIBAJ&sjid=eOoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5125%2C5159521 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon|agency=Associated Press |last=Cour |first=Jim |title=Penalty hits UW; James resigns|date=August 23, 1993|page=1A}}</ref><ref name=tfstm>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=oaIpAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NfEDAAAAIBAJ&pg=4847%2C3036022 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington|agency=(Seattle Times)|last=Farrey |first=Tom |title=Riding hot seat at UW |date=August 24, 1993 |page=C1}}</ref><ref name=uwhdco>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=oKIpAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NfEDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5975%2C2749717 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |last=Boling|first=Dave |title=UW head coach quits over sanctions |date=August 23, 1993 |page=A1}}</ref> Although several other Huskies players were implicated in improprieties, Hobert became the most well-known face of the sanctions, leading to him receiving death threats.<ref name=ST062002/><ref name=lathbem>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=oaIpAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NfEDAAAAIBAJ&pg=2710%2C3034498 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington|agency=(Los Angeles Times)|last=Noland |first=Eric |title=Hobert bemoans sanctions |date=August 24, 1993 |page=C1}}</ref>

Hobert was the 58th pick in the [[1993 NFL draft]], selected in the third round by the [[1993 Los Angeles Raiders season|Los Angeles Raiders]], sixty picks ahead of fellow Husky quarterback Brunell.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1993 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1993/draft.htm |access-date=March 31, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was the third quarterback selected in the draft, behind the top two overall picks, [[Drew Bledsoe]] and [[Rick Mirer]]. Hobert was also selected in the sixteenth round (453rd overall) of the [[1993 Major League Baseball Draft|1993 MLB draft]] by the [[1993 Chicago White Sox season|Chicago White Sox]], but chose to pursue a career in the NFL.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.baseball-reference.com/draft/?query_type=year_round&year_ID=1993&draft_round=16&draft_type=junreg& | title=1993 MLB Draft, 16th round}}</ref>

Hobert was a back-up quarterback for four seasons with the Raiders, then went on to play for the [[Buffalo Bills]] in [[1997 Buffalo Bills season|1997]]. He was initially expected to compete with [[Alex Van Pelt]] and [[Todd Collins (quarterback)|Todd Collins]] for the starting quarterback position made vacant by [[Jim Kelly]]'s retirement; however, after a notorious incident in Buffalo where he publicly admitted that he had not read his playbook and was unprepared to play, he was promptly released in mid-October.<ref name=ST062002/><ref name=bwunpho>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-oct-16-sp-43372-story.html |work=Los Angeles Times |agency=Associated Press |title=Bills waive unprepared Hobert |date=October 16, 1997 |access-date=October 6, 2017}}</ref> Hobert was acquired later that season by the [[New Orleans Saints]], where he remained through [[1999 New Orleans Saints season|1999]]; he signed with the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in [[2000 Indianapolis Colts season|2000]]. While on the Colts roster for two years, he did not play a snap during the regular season.

==Personal life==
Hobert grew up in [[Orting, Washington]].

Hobert has five children.  Hobert became a [[Born again (Christianity)|born again Christian]] during the Saints pre-season camp in 1998.<ref name=ST062002/>

'''William George Pickel''' (born November 5, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] for 12 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Los Angeles Raiders]] from 1983 to 1990 and [[New York Jets]] from 1991 to 1994. Pickel attended [[St. Francis Prep]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Rutgers Scarlet Knights football|Rutgers Scarlet Knights]]. As a second-round draft pick of the Raiders in [[1983 NFL draft|1983]], Pickel overcame injuries to win a [[Super Bowl]] as a [[rookie]], and was a [[Quarterback sack|sack]] threat during the early part of his career with the Raiders, making the 1985 [[All-Pro]] team. He is currently 98th in career sacks with 56. A standout player, Pickel played nearly every Raider defensive snap in 1984 and 1985. He had a distinctive 4-point stance, placing two hands down instead of the usual one, as was the case with other quick defensive tackles such as [[Bob Lilly]] and [[Tom Keating (American football)|Tom Keating]].

Pickel guest starred in a 1994 episode of ''[[Home Improvement (TV series)|Home Improvement]]''[https://web.archive.org/web/20070929023021/http://www.hiarchive.co.uk/episode.php?s=3&e=18]. He is noted for his volunteer work with the [https://web.archive.org/web/20070928083456/http://www.joshuafrase.org/events02.html Joshua Frase Foundation], a [[non-profit]] group that supports research for [[centronuclear myopathy]].

'''Billy Leon Jenkins Jr.''' (born July 8, 1974, in [[Los Angeles]], [[California]]) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]]. After playing [[college football]] for the [[Howard Bison football|Howard Bison]], he played in the NFL for the [[St. Louis Rams]] (1997–1999), [[Denver Broncos]] (2000–2001), [[Green Bay Packers]] (2001), and [[Buffalo Bills]] (2002). He played in [[Super Bowl XXXIV]] for the Rams where he started at safety. After the 1999 season, the Rams traded Jenkins to the Denver Broncos for a fifth-round pick in the 2000 NFL Draft.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/a20dcd101c4e3a0ce5cec21e88b463d2|title = Broncos Sign Rams' Billy Jenkins|website = [[Associated Press]]}}</ref>

He is an alumnus of [[Howard University]]. 
Jenkins is currently a defensive backs coach at his alma mater.

'''William Thomas Simpson''' (born December 5, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1974 to 1982. Before his NFL career, he played defensive back and punted for [[Michigan State University]] and was selected by the [[Los Angeles Rams]] in the second round of the [[1974 NFL draft]]. He was a standout athlete at [[Shrine Catholic High School|Royal Oak Shrine High School]] and was elected to the Archdiocese of Detroit Catholic High School League Hall of Fame in 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aodonline.org/ |title=Archdiocese of Detroit |access-date=2022-06-28 |archive-date=2012-02-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120226081507/http://www.aodonline.org/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Professional career==
Simpson played five seasons with the [[Los Angeles Rams]] (1974–1978) which culminated in his receiving several postseason awards. He finished his pro career with the [[Buffalo Bills]] (1980–1982), retiring with 34 interceptions and 9 more in postseason play.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/ |title=Home |website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref>

During the [[1981–82 NFL playoffs#AFC: Buffalo Bills 31, New York Jets 27|1981 Wild Card playoff game]], played on December 27, 1981, at [[Shea Stadium]], Simpson intercepted a pass near the end zone in the closing seconds of the game to preserve a win for the Bills over the [[1981 New York Jets season|New York Jets]]

==Personal life==
Simpson is the father of [[Brett Simpson]], a 2009 and 2010 [[US Open of Surfing]] champion.

'''William Doughty Andrews Jr.''' (born June 14, 1945) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for 11 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Cleveland Browns]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Southeastern Louisiana Lions football|Southeastern Louisiana Lions]].

Andrews scored his only NFL [[touchdown]] in the first ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' game televised by [[ABC Sports|ABC]] on September 21, [[1970 NFL season|1970]]. Late in the fourth quarter, Andrews [[Interception|intercepted]] a pass by the [[New York Jets]]' [[Joe Namath]] and returned it 25 yards for a touchdown to secure the Browns' 31–21 victory.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Reed |first1=Tom |title=The first hero of 'Monday Night Football': How one interception changed the life of Billy Andrews |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1264729/2019/10/03/the-first-hero-of-monday-night-football-how-one-interception-changed-the-life-of-billy-andrews/ |access-date=14 June 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=3 October 2019}}</ref>

He now lives in [[Bluff Creek, Louisiana]], a small community outside of Clinton.

'''William Abb Cannon Jr.''' (born October 8, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas A&M Aggies football|Texas A&M Aggies]].

==Early life==
Cannon  attended [[Broadmoor High School]] where he lettered in four sports. In baseball, he played [[shortstop]] and was a two-time All-State and an [[All-American]] selection. In [[American football|football]] he played [[quarterback]], [[running back]], [[Safety (American and Canadian football position)|safety]], [[special teams]] and even kicked a few times. In his senior year, he received All-State and [[All-American]] honors, while helping his team to an undefeated regular season.

On Halloween night in 1979, he returned a punt against Istrouma (his father's alma mater) 89 yards for a [[touchdown]] and a 20–18 win, exactly 20 years after his father had [[Billy Cannon's Halloween Run|his famous 89 yard punt return]] for [[LSU Tigers football|Louisiana State University]] to beat [[Ole Miss Rebels football|Ole Miss]] 7–3.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sports World Specials Cannon's Best Shot |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/04/20/sports/by-jim-benagh.html |access-date=March 5, 2020 |website=New York Times}}</ref>

As an 18-year-old senior with ability and a marquee name, he was a probable first-round draft choice in the [[1980 Major League Baseball draft]] as a [[shortstop]]/[[outfielder]]. His father had previously sent telegrams to all major league teams advising not to invest a draft selection on his son, because he was going to attend college.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1817&dat=19800614&id=hjAdAAAAIBAJ&pg=6668,3515217 | title=Grievances issued in Cannon drafting | access-date=March 5, 2020}}</ref> After the [[New York Yankees]] drafted him in the third round, teams filed grievances citing that they were misled by the telegrams, while there were secret meetings with the Yankees to negotiate a contract agreement. Then [[baseball]] commissioner [[Bowie Kuhn]] vetoed the contract, forfeited the Yankees draft pick and called for a special draft to be held for his rights.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1891&dat=19800627&id=k0JHAAAAIBAJ&pg=2905,4507698 | title=Yanks lose draft pick of Cannon | access-date=March 5, 2020}}</ref> The [[Cleveland Indians]] selected Cannon in the special draft.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2199&dat=19800816&id=eJYyAAAAIBAJ&pg=4756,3363918 | title=Draft rights of Cannon given to Tribe by Kuhn | access-date=March 5, 2020}}</ref>

==College career==
After the Yankees selection was voided, he committed to [[Texas A&M University]] to the dismay of [[LSU]] fans.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1243&dat=19800730&id=fvxXAAAAIBAJ&pg=4641,3891348 | title=Cannon signs as Aggie | access-date=March 5, 2020}}</ref> As a freshman, he started 6 games as a [[Flanker (American football)|flanker]], making 11 receptions for 118 yards (fourth on the team). He ranked second in the conference in kickoff returns with a 20.8-yard average.

As a sophomore, he was moved to [[free safety]] and led the secondary with 58 tackles.

As a junior, he played at [[strong safety]], while registering 64 tackles (fifth on the team). He finished third in the conference in punt returns with a 9-yard average on 31 returns.

As a senior, he was switched to [[outside linebacker]], but even then as a key member of the defense, he still returned kicks and punts. He posted 60 tackles (seventh on the team), 4 sacks and 3 fumble recoveries. He finished his college career with 86 punt returns for a 7.6-yard average, one punt return touchdown and 22 kickoff returns for a 21.1-yard average.

He also was a starter in the outfield for the [[baseball]] team. He was drafted by the [[Los Angeles Dodgers]].

==Professional career==
Cannon was selected by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in the first round (25th overall) of the [[1984 NFL draft]], becoming the first player from [[Texas A&M University]] drafted by the Cowboys.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1984/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-10 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Texas A&M Drafted Players/Alumni |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/schools/texasam/drafted.htm |access-date=2025-07-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> It was reported that the [[Washington Redskins]] also had him as their desired selection in the round. He was also selected by the [[San Antonio Gunslingers (USFL team)|San Antonio Gunslingers]] in the [[1984 USFL Territorial Draft]].

Eight games into his rookie season, he was a reserve right [[outside linebacker]] alternating with [[Anthony Dickerson]], when an existing congenital spinal condition was complicated after he tackled [[New Orleans Saints]] [[running back]] [[Wayne Wilson (American football)|Wayne Wilson]]. He was knocked unconscious, suffered damage to two vertebrae near his neck and experienced a brief paralysis of his arms and legs. He never started and appeared in just eight games before this injury forced him to retire in order to avoid risking paralysis.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-04-28-sp-21464-story.html|title=THE ORDEAL OF THE CANNONS : Billy Jr. Is the Son of a Famous Father Now in Prison and He Is Lucky to Have Survived Severe Neck Injury|work=latimes}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=348&dat=19850328&id=spBOAAAAIBAJ&pg=4298,5787244 | title=Cannon's grid career in doubt | access-date=March 5, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Cannon filed a multimillion-dollar lawsuit claiming negligence by the Cowboys, after he informed them of experiencing numbness in his upper body when making tackles. The team denied ever receiving such claims but settled in 1992.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1817&dat=19861020&id=SDQdAAAAIBAJ&pg=2137,7447391 | title=Billy Cannon Jr. suing the Cowboys | access-date=March 5, 2020}}</ref>

His father, [[Billy Cannon]], was a [[Heisman Trophy]] winner who played in the [[American Football League]].

'''Paul William Troup III''' (April 2, 1951 – December 14, 2013) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player. He was born in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]]. An undrafted [[quarterback]] from the [[University of South Carolina]],  Troup played in seven [[NFL]] seasons from 1974 to 1980 for 2 different teams. He saw his most extensive action for the Colts in 1978, when Bert Jones was injured and Mike Kirkland ineffective.<ref>{{Citation| url =https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TrouBi00.htm?redir | title =Player| publisher = Pro-Football Reference.com| accessdate =7 June 2012}}</ref>

After being released by Baltimore, Troup went north to the [[Canadian Football League|Canadian Football League's]] [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]], where he served as the backup to starter [[Dieter Brock]] for the [[1979 Winnipeg Blue Bombers season|1979 season]].

'''William Campfield''' (born August 20, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] and the [[New York Giants]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Kansas Jayhawks football|Kansas Jayhawks]] and was selected in the 11th round of the [[1978 NFL draft]]. He played in [[Super Bowl XV]] with the Eagles in 1981.

==Early life==
Campfield graduated from [[Derby High School (Kansas)|Derby High School]] in [[Derby, Kansas]], in 1974. He was a four-year letterman as a running back at the [[University of Kansas]], averaging over six yards every time he touched the ball and scoring 12 career touchdowns.

==Professional career==

===Philadelphia Eagles===
Campfield was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the eleventh round of the [[1978 NFL draft]]. He was waived on August 22, 1983.<ref>{{cite news |title=Campfield is cut by Philadelphia |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=KpwyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=--gFAAAAIBAJ&pg=6837,5134543 |newspaper=Lawrence Journal-World |date=August 23, 1983 |accessdate=2010-03-30}}</ref>

===New York Giants===
Campfield was claimed off waivers by the [[New York Giants]], and he was released a week later on August 29, 1983.<ref>{{cite news |title=Back surgery for Spagnola; Eagles cut 10 |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=9dkxAAAAIBAJ&sjid=6uQFAAAAIBAJ&pg=2088,8955141 |newspaper=Reading Eagle |date=August 30, 1983 |accessdate=2010-03-30}}</ref>

===San Antonio Gunslingers===
Campfield signed a one-year contract with the [[San Antonio Gunslingers (USFL team)|San Antonio Gunslingers]], and one week later, on March 6, 1984, announced his retirement.<ref>{{cite news |title=Armed with package, Schaefer seeks meeting with Colts' Irsay |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=rdI_AAAAIBAJ&sjid=qeMFAAAAIBAJ&pg=4818,6627585 |newspaper=Reading Eagle |date=March 9, 1984 |accessdate=2010-03-30}}</ref>

===Arizona Outlaws===
Campfield came out of retirement and signed with the [[Arizona Outlaws]] on February 12, 1985.<ref>{{cite news |title=Outlaws Sign Campfield |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=vRgVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NwYEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4337,8877699 |newspaper=Ocala Star-Banner |date=February 15, 1985 |accessdate=2010-03-30}}</ref>

'''William Latsko ''' (born February 16, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[fullback (American football)|fullback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[University of Florida]], and was a member of a [[BCS National Championship Game|BCS National Championship]] team.  Thereafter, he was signed by the NFL's [[Carolina Panthers]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2007, and was also a member of the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] and [[San Diego Chargers]] of the NFL, and the [[Virginia Destroyers]] of the [[United Football League (2009–)|United Football League]] (UFL).

== Early life ==
William Latsko was born on February 16, 1984 in [[Gainesville, Florida]].<ref name="pfr"/> He played [[high school football]] at [[Buchholz High School]] in Gainesville as a [[linebacker]].<ref name="bio">{{cite web | url=http://www.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2006&player_id=54 | title=Billy Latsko | publisher=gatorzone.com | accessdate=8 November 2024 | archive-date=September 24, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924040404/http://www.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2006&player_id=54 | url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref> He was a three-year starter and was named third-team all-state in 2000, second-team all-state in 2001, and first-team all-area in 2001.<ref name="bio"/> Latsko was also a leftfielder on the baseball team for four years.<ref name="bio"/> He was on the weightlifting team for four years as well and set the school record for the [[clean and jerk]] (325 lbs).<ref name="bio"/>

== College career ==
Latsko joined the [[Florida Gators football|Florida Gators]] of the [[University of Florida]] as a [[Walk-on (sports)|walk-on]] in 2002.<ref name="gainesville">{{cite web | url=https://www.gainesville.com/story/news/2005/10/14/h-back-latsko-has-gritty-style/31463289007/ | title=H-back Latsko has gritty style | publisher=gainesville.com | date=October 14, 2005 | accessdate=8 November 2024 | author=Brockway, Kevin}}</ref> He was [[redshirted]] his first year in 2002 and spent the year working with the [[scout team]] at [[middle linebacker]].<ref name="bio"/> He played in all 13 games during the 2003 season as the team's main [[fullback (American football)|fullback]], rushing three times for 14 yards and catching two passes for 31 yards in 102 total offensive snaps that season.<ref name="bio"/> He also led the team that year with 10 [[special teams]] tackles.<ref name="bio"/>

Latsko earned an athletic scholarship in February 2004.<ref name="gainesville"/> He was the team's primary fullback again in 2004 and appeared in all 12 games, starting three. He totaled 11 receptions for 76 yards and two touchdowns.<ref name="bio"/> He also led the team with 248 special team snaps and was named to the [[Southeastern Conference|SEC]] Academic Honor Roll.<ref name="bio"/> Latsko spent time on offense, defense (linebacker), and special teams in 2005, playing in all 12 games while recording 5 catches for 43 yards and one touchdown, and eight total tackles on defense.<ref name="bio"/>

Latsko appeared in all 14 games during his senior year in 2006, catching four passes for 38 yards.<ref name="bio"/> The Gators defeated the [[2006 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State Buckeyes]] to win the [[2007 BCS National Championship Game|BCS National Championship]] that season.<ref name="bio"/>  He majored in building construction.<ref name="bio"/>

== Professional career ==
After going undrafted in the [[2007 NFL draft]], Latsko signed with the [[Carolina Panthers]] on May 4, 2007.<ref name="pfr"/> He was waived on September 1, signed to the team's [[practice squad]] on September 3, released on October 2, and re-signed to the practice squad again on October 9.<ref name="pfr"/> He was promoted to the active roster on November 6 but was waived again on November 10 and signed to the practice squad on November 13, 2007.<ref name="pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LatsBi00.htm | title=Billy Latsko | publisher=pro-football-reference.com | accessdate=8 November 2024}}</ref>

Latsko signed a reserve/future contract with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] on January 14, 2008, and was later waived on August 30, 2008.<ref name="pfr"/>

He was signed to the Panthers' practice squad on September 1, 2008 and was released on September 30, 2008.<ref name="pfr"/>

Latsko was signed to the practice squad of the [[San Diego Chargers]] on October 15, 2008.<ref name="pfr"/> He was promoted to the active roster on November 29, but did not play in any games for the team during the 2008 season.<ref name="pfr"/> He was waived on September 5, 2009, and signed to the practice squad two days later on September 7, where he spent the remainder of the 2009 season.<ref name="pfr"/> Latsko signed a reserve/future contract with the Chargers on January 29, 2010.<ref name="pfr"/> He was waived by the Chargers on September 4 but was later re-signed on December 30, 2010.<ref name="pfr"/> He made his NFL debut, and only career appearance, on January 2, 2011 against the [[Denver Broncos]] and recorded one solo tackle.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LatsBi00/gamelog/2010/ | title=Billy Latsko | publisher=pro-football-reference.com | accessdate=8 November 2024}}</ref> Latsko became a free agent after the 2010 season on July 26, 2011, the first day after the [[2011 NFL lockout]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://profootballarchives.com/transactions/l/lats00100.html | title=Billy Latsko NFL Transactions | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=8 November 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/topics/_/page/nfl-labor-negotiations | title=NFL Lockout | publisher=espn.com | date=December 5, 2012 | accessdate=8 November 2024}}</ref>

Latsko was signed by the [[Virginia Destroyers]] of the [[United Football League (2009–)|United Football League]] on May 19, 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/?id=4206233 |title=UFL Transactions |work=OurSports Central |date=May 19, 2011 |access-date=June 14, 2011}}</ref> He started all four games for the Destroyers during the 2011 season, catching four passes for 16 yards and one touchdown while also making one tackle.<ref name="pfa"/> On October 21, 2011, the Destroyers defeated the [[Las Vegas Locomotives]] in the [[2011 UFL championship game]] by a score of 17–3.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://profootballarchives.com/2011uflvir.html | title=2011 Virginia Destroyers (UFL) | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=8 November 2024}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Latsko's grandfather, Bill Latsko, was a quarterback for the [[1940 Florida Gators football team|1940 Florida Gators]].<ref name="bio"/>

'''William Augusta Davis III''' (born July 6, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and [[Baltimore Ravens]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh Panthers]].

==Early life==
Davis attended [[Irvin High School]], where he played as a [[quarterback]], [[defensive back]] and punter. As a senior, he passed for 1,200 yards, receiving All-district, All-city and All-region honors. In [[track & field|track]], he competed in the [[pole vault]], [[100 metres]] and [[200 metres]], receiving All-district and All-city honors.

He accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. As a freshman, he was converted into a [[wide receiver]], posting  11 receptions for 100 yards. As a sophomore, he collected 34 receptions for 503 yards (14.8-yard average) and 3 [[touchdown]]s.

As a junior, he started 9 out of 11 games, registering 24 receptions for 346 yards (14.4-yard average) with one [[touchdown]].

As a senior, he led the team with 51 receptions for 731 yards (14.3-yard average) and 9 [[touchdown]]s. He tied a school record with 4 [[touchdown]] receptions in a game, to help upset [[Rutgers University]], while also making 10 receptions for 135 yards.

He finished with 120 receptions (third in school history) for 1,680 yards (fifth in school history) and 13 [[touchdown]]s.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://apnews.com/3bc85a72f90ffd13aebcf2da6ee63d76 | title=Davis would like to make Steelers pay for overlooking him | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

==Professional career==

===Dallas Cowboys===
Davis was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] after the [[1995 NFL draft]]. He made the roster based on his [[special teams]] play. He recorded 16 [[special teams]] tackles (fifth on the team) and was a part of the [[Super Bowl XXX]] winning team.

In [[1996 NFL season|1996]], he missed 3 games with a broken fifth metatarsal in his right foot. He made 17 [[special teams]] tackles (tied for third on the team).

In [[1997 NFL season|1997]], he finished third on the team with 20 [[special teams]] tackles. As a [[wide receiver]], he was mostly a reserve player that was known to have excellent training camps where he showed his explosiveness and size advantages, but it didn't transfer to the regular season.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19980805&id=Nx1IAAAAIBAJ&sjid=HYEMAAAAIBAJ&pg=5445,5510454 | title=Davis craving attention | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

In [[1998 NFL season|1998]] with the arrival of new [[head coach]] [[Chan Gailey]], he was named the starter opposite to future hall of famer [[Michael Irvin]] and proceeded to have 39 receptions for 691 yards (17.7-yard average) and 3 [[touchdown]]s.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1999/06/16/ravens-close-to-landing-b-davis-cowboys-receiver-could-sign-today-boulware-begins-rehab/ | title=Ravens close to landing B. Davis | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref> He also had 11 [[special teams]] tackles.

On May 31, [[1999 NFL season|1999]], he was waived for salary-cap reasons after the signing of [[free agent]] [[Raghib Ismail]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/cowboys-release-wr-davis/ | title=Cowboys Release WR Davis | website=[[CBS News]] | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

===Baltimore Ravens===
In [[1999 NFL season|1999]], he struggled while playing on offense, but it didn't affect his [[special teams]] play, finishing with a career-best 21 tackles. The next year, he finished fourth on the team with 15 [[special teams]] tackles and was a part of the [[Super Bowl XXXV]] winning side.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2001/08/15/champs-hope-thompson-is-special/ | title=Champs hope Thompson is special | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref> He was released for salary cap reasons on March 19, [[2001 NFL season|2001]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2001/03/20/offer-to-sharper-in-question/ | title=Offer to Sharper in question | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

===Chicago Bears===
On August 30, [[2001 NFL season|2001]], he signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[Chicago Bears]], who were looking to replace an injured [[Frankie Smith (American football)|Frankie Smith]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2001/08/31/robinson-on-track-for-return-to-lineup/ | title=Robinson on track for return to lineup | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref> He was cut on September first.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://articles.baltimoresun.com/2001-09-02/sports/0109020211_1_james-burgess-ol-wr | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141031032644/http://articles.baltimoresun.com/2001-09-02/sports/0109020211_1_james-burgess-ol-wr | url-status=dead | archive-date=October 31, 2014 | title=Football Bears: Released RB Marlon Barnes, DL Van... | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

===Oakland Raiders===
On May 30, [[2002 NFL season|2002]], Davis signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[Oakland Raiders]]. He was waived on August 26.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://articles.chicagotribune.com/2002-08-27/sports/0208270231_1_contract-dt-emarlos-leroy-signed | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141031043258/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/2002-08-27/sports/0208270231_1_contract-dt-emarlos-leroy-signed | url-status=dead | archive-date=October 31, 2014 | title=Recalled INF... | access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

'''William Jeffrey Thomas''' (born August 7, 1949) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[Houston Oilers]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs]].  He was selected by the Cowboys in the first round of the [[1972 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Boston College Eagles football|Boston College Eagles]].

==Early life==
Thomas attended [[Peekskill High School]], before accepting a football scholarship from [[Boston College]]. In April 1970, he dislocated his left shoulder playing [[basketball]], so he had to wear a harness during the [[American football|football]] season, until he was forced to have surgery and miss one game.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://newspapers.bc.edu/cgi-bin/bostonsh?a=d&d=bcheights19700929.2.94&srpos=1&e=-------en-20--1--txt-IN-bill+thomas+shoulder---- | title=Thomas plays despite shoulder separation | accessdate=February 28, 2018}}</ref> In 1971, he helped the school achieve their best record (9-2) in a season since 1954, while posting 119 carries for 598 yards and 2 [[touchdown]]s.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bill-thomas-2.html | title=College Stats | accessdate=February 28, 2018}}</ref>

His versatility running and blocking was valued by the team, so he spent his playing time between the [[Halfback (American football)|halfback]] and [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] positions. Fighting through injuries for most of his college career, he recorded a total of 931 career rushing yards (4.5-yard average), 2 [[touchdown]]s and was never the leading rusher on his team. He also [[Letterman (sports)|lettered]] in [[track and field|track]] and ran the [[200 metres]].

==Professional career==

===Dallas Cowboys===
Coming off their [[Super Bowl VI]] win, the [[Dallas Cowboys]] entered the [[1972 NFL draft]] worried about the future of [[Duane Thomas]] and the injury history of [[Calvin Hill]], so they focused on their [[running back]] depth. With their first round draft choice the team selected Thomas, who was ranked sixth overall on their draft board and with their second draft choice they selected [[Robert Newhouse]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1314&dat=19720202&id=etkvAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Su0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=7379,440578 | title=Cowboys 'Stole' Runners | accessdate=February 28, 2018}}</ref>

He never fully recovered from the left shoulder injury he suffered in college and re-injured it during a dummy blocking drill in [[training camp]]. He went through surgery to repair the staple pin that was used to secure the shoulder in the original operation and was placed on injured reserve. He was activated for the eighth game of the [[1972 NFL season|1972 season]], touching the ball only twice as a rookie during [[Kickoff (gridiron football)|kickoff]] returns.

On September 28, [[1973 NFL season|1973]], he was waived due to his lack of progress and his injury history and to make room for [[running back]] [[Cyril Pinder]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19730929&id=mqBHAAAAIBAJ&sjid=rn8MAAAAIBAJ&pg=4211,4459501 | title=Cowboys Waive Back; Acquire Cyril Pender | accessdate=February 28, 2018}}</ref>

===Houston Oilers===
On October 1, [[1973 NFL season|1973]], the [[Houston Oilers]] claimed him off waivers and played a reserve role during the season.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19731002&id=_jAcAAAAIBAJ&sjid=OFoEAAAAIBAJ&pg=2580,171822 | title=Thomas Now Houston Oiler Running Back | accessdate=February 28, 2018}}</ref> On August 16, [[1974 NFL season|1974]], he was traded to the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in exchange for a seventh-round draft choice (#162-Mike Biehle).<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19740817&id=97xdAAAAIBAJ&sjid=I14NAAAAIBAJ&pg=4809,2469381 | title=Hargett Traded To Detroit | accessdate=February 28, 2018}}</ref>

===Kansas City Chiefs===
In [[1974 NFL season|1974]], he experienced some success playing [[special teams]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]], returning 25 [[Kickoff (gridiron football)|kickoffs]] for 571 yards. He was waived on August 2, [[1975 NFL season|1975]].

==Personal life==
Thomas was a teacher for more than 27 years, while also serving as coach and administrator at Madison Park High School and Gavin Middle School. He also had a stint with the [[American football|football]] coaching staff of [[Northeastern University]].

'''William Morton Lyon''' (born December 10, 1973) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive lineman]] for the [[Green Bay Packers]] and [[Minnesota Vikings]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Marshall Thundering Herd football|Marshall Thundering Herd]]. He signed with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] after going undrafted in 1997 but was waived before the start of the regular season. Lyon later joined the Packers' practice squad in 1997 and played in 59 games for the team from 1998 to 2002. He also appeared in 13 games for the Minnesota Vikings in 2003.

==Early life==
William Morton Lyon was born on December 10, 1973, in [[Ashland, Kentucky]].<ref name="Pfr"/> He attended [[Lloyd Memorial High School]] in [[Erlanger, Kentucky]].<ref name="Pfa">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/l/lyon00100.html | title=Billy Lyon | publisher=Pro Football Archives | accessdate=6 October 2024}}</ref>

==College career==
Lyon played [[college football]] for the [[Marshall Thundering Herd football|Marshall Thundering Herd]] from 1993 to 1996 and was a three-year starter.<ref name="Pfa"/><ref name="Marsh">{{cite web | url=https://herdzone.com/honors/marshall-athletics-hall-of-fame/billy-lyon/142 | title=Billy Lyon | publisher=herdzone.com | accessdate=6 October 2024}}</ref> He was [[redshirted]] in 1992 as the team won the national championship.<ref name="Pfa"/><ref name="Marsh"/> Lyon helped the Thundering Herd advance to the national championship game his junior year in 1995 by recording a career-high 13 tackles, including one safety, in the team's semifinal victory over [[McNeese Cowboys football|McNeese State]].<ref name="Marsh"/> He totaled 91 tackles and nine sacks his senior season in 1996 as the Thundering Herd went 15–0 and won the national championship.<ref name="Marsh"/>

Lyon was inducted into the Marshall Athletic Hall of Fame in 2007.<ref name="Marsh"/>

==Professional career==
===Kansas City Chiefs===
After going undrafted in the [[1997 NFL draft]], Lyon signed with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] on April 28, 1997. He was waived on August 15, 1997.<ref name="transactions">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/l/lyon00100.html | title=Billy Lyon NFL Transactions | publisher=Pro Football Archives | accessdate=6 October 2024}}</ref>

===Green Bay Packers===
Lyon was signed to the practice squad of the [[Green Bay Packers]] on November 20, 1997. He re-signed with the team on January 28, 1998.<ref name="transactions"/> He appeared in four games in 1998, recording four solo tackles, two assisted tackles, and one sack.<ref name="Pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LyonBi20.htm | title=Billy Lyon | publisher=Pro-Football-Reference | accessdate=6 October 2024}}</ref> Lyon also appeared in one playoff game that year but recorded no statistics.<ref name="Pfr"/>

Lyon appeared in all 16 games, starting four, for the Packers in 1999, accumulating 12 solo tackles, seven assisted tackles, two sacks, one interception, and two pass breakups. He played in 11 games, starting one, during the 2000 season, recording seven solo tackles, four assisted tackles, and one sack.<ref name="Pfr"/>

He played in 12 games in 2001, totaling 13 solo tackles, six assisted tackles, two sacks, one forced fumble, and one pass breakup. He also appeared in two playoff games that season and made three solo tackles.<ref name="Pfr"/>

Lyon played in 16 games, starting two, during his final season for the Packers in 2002, recording 11 solo tackles, four assisted tackles, and two sacks.<ref name="Pfr"/> He became a free agent after the 2002 season.<ref name="transactions"/>

Overall, he appeared in 59 regular season games, starting seven, for the Packers, and made 70 combined tackles and eight sacks.<ref name="Pfr"/>

===Minnesota Vikings===
Lyon signed with the [[Minnesota Vikings]] on March 5, 2003. He appeared in 13 games for the Vikings during the 2003, accumulating four solo tackles and one assisted tackle.<ref name="Pfr"/> He was released  on August 31, 2004.<ref name="Pfr"/>

'''William Henry Olds''' (born February 21, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for four seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-baltimore-sun/176863667/ | title=The case of fullback Bill Olds | work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] | date=August 19, 1975 | accessdate=17 July 2025 | author=Snyder, Cameron, C. | pages=C3}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska Cornhuskers]] and was selected by the [[Baltimore Colts]] in the third round of the [[1973 NFL draft]] with the 61st overall pick. He played in the NFL for the Colts, [[Seattle Seahawks]], and [[Philadelphia Eagles]].

==Nebraska Cornhuskers==
Olds graduated from high school in 1969 and played [[college football]] for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska Cornhuskers]] under [[head coach]] [[Bob Devaney]], with future head coach [[Tom Osborne]] as [[offensive coordinator]].  He was the [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] in the [[I formation]], the lead blocker for [[Halfback (American football)|tailback]]s [[Jeff Kinney (American football)|Jeff Kinney]] and [[Johnny Rodgers]], the [[1972 NCAA University Division football season|1972]] [[Heisman Trophy]] winner. Nebraska won [[NCAA Division I FBS National Football Championship|national championships]] in [[1970 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|1970]] and [[1971 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|1971]], and a third straight [[1973 Orange Bowl|Orange Bowl]] following the [[1972 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|1972]] season to finish at fourth in the AP poll. The Huskers went 33–2–2 (.919) in those three seasons (1970–72).

'''William Dominic Austin''' (born March 8, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

He graduated from [[Kempner High School]] in [[Sugar Land, Texas]]. He played [[college football]] at [[New Mexico Lobos football|New Mexico]]. He attended the [[University of New Mexico]] from 1993 to 1997 and was an All-Conference [[defensive back]] his sophomore, junior, and senior years. He played for the [[Indianapolis Colts]] from 1998, 1999, 2000 and was a part of the [[AFC East]] Championship team in 1999.

He currently resides in [[Houston]], Texas.

==After football==

After being diagnosed with stage 4 [[cancer]], Austin launched the Tackles 4 Cancer nonprofit. His mission to assist other cancer patients with transportation to and from their treatments served as the fundamental mission of the organization. Now cancer-free, he has hosted over 20 events with celebrities and was featured as an inspirational figure by [[Beyonce]]'s BeGood Foundation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.beyonce.com/inspiration-dominic-austin/|title=Beyonce Names Billy Dominic Austin an Inspiration (BeGood Foundation)|last=Austin|first=Billy|date=2017-11-21|website=www.beyonce.com/inspiration-dominic-austin/|accessdate=2017-11-21|archive-date=2017-05-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170514175948/http://www.beyonce.com/inspiration-dominic-austin/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''William Oliver Roe II''' (February 6, 1958 – September 13, 2003) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and [[New Orleans Saints]]. He also was a member of the [[Boston Breakers (USFL)|Boston Breakers]], [[Memphis Showboats]] and [[Birmingham Stallions]] in the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Colorado Buffaloes football|Colorado Buffaloes]].

==Early life==
Roe attended [[Thornwood High School]], where he practiced football, [[basketball]], [[baseball]] and [[track & field|track]]. He accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Colorado Boulder]]. He became a starter at [[inside linebacker]] as a junior and received honorable mention [[Big Eight Conference|All-Big Eight]] honors.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2199&dat=19781121&id=yoQyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=zOYFAAAAIBAJ&pg=6456,4626198 | title=Sooners dominate All-Big Eight | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> He lost the final 3 games with a right knee injury, which required offseason surgery.

As a senior, he received [[List of All-Big Eight Conference football teams|All-Big Eight]] honors, after leading the conference in tackles (162) and the team in interceptions (3).<ref>{{cite web | url=https://cubuffs.com/sports/2011/7/14/buffs-forever-obituaries.aspx | title=Buffs For Ever | accessdate=February 19, 2018 | url-status=dead | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303215449/http://www.cubuffs.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=600&ATCLID=205181990 | archivedate=March 3, 2016 }}</ref> He also had 10 tackles for loss, 3 sacks and 10 or more tackles in seven games, becoming the first player to win [[Big Eight Conference|Big Eight]] Defensive Player of the Week honors two weeks in a row (Nov. 17 and Nov. 24). He posted 12 unassisted tackles and one sack against the [[University of Kansas]]. He registered 18 tackles against the [[University of Missouri]]. He returned an interception for a 69-yard [[touchdown]] against [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska]]. His best game came against [[Kansas State University]], when he registered 24 tackles (second most in school history) and 2 interceptions.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2199&dat=19791125&id=HagyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=CucFAAAAIBAJ&pg=3181,5588371 | title=Buffs belt Wildcats, 21-6 | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> In 1978, he won the school's heavyweight boxing championship.

==Professional career==

===Dallas Cowboys===
After the [[Dallas Cowboys]] entered the [[1980 NFL draft]] without their first and second round draft choices (traded to the [[Baltimore Colts]] for [[John Dutton (defensive lineman)|John Dutton]]), the team made Roe their first selection in the third round (78th overall).<ref>{{Cite web |title=1980 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1980/draft.htm |access-date=2025-08-13 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> As a rookie, he played mainly on [[special teams]].

On August 24, [[1981 NFL season|1981]], he was placed on the [[injured reserve list]] with a sprained ankle.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2245&dat=19810825&id=i-MzAAAAIBAJ&sjid=QTIHAAAAIBAJ&pg=4383,6862249 | title=Cowboys lacking in consistency | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> He was released on September 3, [[1982 NFL season|1982]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19820904&id=ysYcAAAAIBAJ&sjid=bFkEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4522,1780581 | title=Pokes Keep Six Rookies | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

===Boston Breakers (USFL)===
In January [[1983 USFL season|1983]], he signed with the [[Denver Gold]] of the [[United States Football League]], which traded him along with the rights to [[Dick Jauron]] to the [[Boston Breakers (USFL)|Boston Breakers]] in February, in exchange for the rights to Tom Davis and an eighth round draft choice.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1817&dat=19830210&id=sjkdAAAAIBAJ&sjid=3aUEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4022,2154696&hl=es | title=Transactions | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> The Breakers named him their starting [[inside linebacker]].

===Memphis Showboats (USFL)===
In [[1984 USFL season|1984]], he was the [[Memphis Showboats]] starting [[inside linebacker]], before being traded in May to the [[Birmingham Stallions]] in exchange for a future draft choice.

===Birmingham Stallions (USFL)===
With the [[Birmingham Stallions]] he was a standout [[linebacker]] on the league's top defense, before the [[United States Football League]] folded.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/07/08/sports/usfl-stars-win-gain-championship-berth.html | title=U.S.F.L.; Stars Win, Gain Championship Berth | work=The New York Times | date=July 8, 1985 | accessdate=February 19, 2018 | last1=Wallace | first1=William N. }}</ref>

===New Orleans Saints===
After the players went on a strike on the third week of the [[1987 NFL season|1987 season]], those contests were canceled (reducing the 16 game season to 15) and the [[National Football League|NFL]] decided that the games would be played with replacement players. Roe was signed to be a part of the [[New Orleans Saints]] replacement team, that was given the mock name "Saint Elsewheres" by the media. He went on to start all three games at [[linebacker]], before being released once the strike ended.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19871003&id=W9FdAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Jl4NAAAAIBAJ&pg=6555,444323&hl=es | title=Rosters Interesting If Nothing Else | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Roe died on September 13, 2003.

'''William Edward Griggs III''' (born August 4, 1962) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[tight end]] for the [[New York Jets]]. Griggs went to college at the [[University of Virginia]] and played [[tight end]] under the legendary UVA head coach [[George Welsh (American football)|George Welsh]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.owlsports.com/coaches.aspx?path=football&rc=519|title = Bill Griggs - Football Coach}}</ref> He played for the Jets from 1984 to 1989, catching 25 passes for 262 yards. His first NFL reception was a touchdown catch in the Jets victory over the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the 1986 playoffs. He served as the offensive line and defensive line coach at [[Pennsauken High School]] in [[Pennsauken, New Jersey]] in 2011.<ref>https://www.linkedin.com/pub/bill-griggs/3a/a39/8a4 {{Self-published source|date=June 2022}}</ref>

Griggs is the older brother of the late former NFL outside linebacker, [[David Griggs (American football)|David Griggs]].
